faq.q: What are good questions to ask yourself at the end of the day?
faq.a: Concrete ones, asked in order: what happened, what you felt and when, what went well and why, what is still open, and the first thing you will do about it tomorrow. Questions about specific events can be answered and put down. Abstract ones like "what's wrong with me?" tend to keep the mind going.

faq.q: Is it good to journal right before bed?
faq.a: It depends on which way the writing faces. In a 2018 sleep-lab study, people who wrote a specific to-do list for five minutes before bed fell asleep faster than people who wrote about tasks they had already finished. Do the looking-back part earlier in the evening and keep the last minutes for open items and next steps.

faq.q: Do gratitude journal prompts actually work?
faq.a: A little. A 2016 meta-analysis found gratitude exercises improved well-being slightly more than neutral activities, but no more than other active exercises, and showed no clear effect on anxiety. One gratitude question is worth keeping if you like it; it shouldn't be your whole routine.

faq.q: Is asking "why" in a journal bad for you?
faq.a: Not always. In a 2005 study by Kross and colleagues, asking why you felt something helped when people pictured the event from an observer's distance. Asking why while mentally reliving the scene is the version that tends to turn into rumination.

faq.q: How long should an evening reflection take?
faq.a: Five to ten minutes is enough. The sleep study that tested bedtime to-do lists used five minutes of writing, and two good questions done most nights are more useful than a long list done for a week.

informationGain: Unlike the top results, which are unsourced lists of interchangeable prompts, this piece sorts evening questions by what the research says each kind does, gives an order to ask them in (looking back early, a specific plan right before bed), names the questions that make things worse, and reports the honest, modest effect sizes for gratitude and writing alone.
